title: Tess and the Deep Core Secret
markdown:
The abyssal waters of Xylos III tasted of old salt and abandoned work. Among the skeletal frames of dead mines, Tess the scavenger diver moved like someone who had learned the currents by bruise and habit. Her fingers coaxed salvage from the watery tomb. Under the practiced calm lived a tremor she never named in reports: not the unseen things below, but the sheer overwhelming nothingness that opened when lights failed. It rode in her gut on every descent, a cold silent passenger.

A glint unlike any other. Not the dull gleam of discarded ore, but a luminescence that pulsed with forgotten vibrant power. Curiosity, a potent force that warred with her lingering dread, propelled Tess forward. The light beckoned in the oppressive murk. She surfaced in a cavernous chamber, walls lined with crystalline panels that hummed with latent energy, a symphony of dormant power. Before her lay an intact precursor lab, a marvel perfectly preserved beneath the waves, untouched by rust.

“Incredible,” breathed Olek, the miner’s son, as he clambered through the breach Tess had forged. His broad frame filled the narrow opening, a stark contrast to Tess’s lithe form. He knew the rock, the tunnels, the very heartbeat of this moon, but this was alien wonder. He ran a gloved hand over a smooth cool panel, his face a mask of pure awe.

“This changes everything,” Tess whispered, her fear momentarily eclipsed. This lab wasn’t just old tech. It felt like a promise, a whisper from a vanished civilization.

Wonder did not last. Water outside shimmered. A submersible arrived, vast and unwelcome.

“Hold. This sector is now under corporate jurisdiction.” Director Thorne’s face was a grim mask behind the viewport. Claim jumpers in sleek suits glided like sharks. Profit, not history.

“They want it all,” Olek muttered, hand on his pick.

“We found it first.” Tess’s protectiveness surprised her. The place felt sacred.

Thorne’s commander, Grish, scoffed. “Local pests. No claim. Stand aside.”

Drones whirred like enraged insects. Lasers kissed the lab’s seals. Walls crackled. A crucial conduit sparked and died. “My gear,” Olek cried. “The EMP fried my comms.” Cut off. Isolated. The easy retreat to the surface was gone.

“Chime, activate.” Tess remembered the small humming sphere near the entrance.

A resonant note cut the drone-whine. A silver sphere unfolded into a compact multi-limbed pressure suit. “Chime online. Designated purpose: Guardian of Precursor Archives.”

“You can understand us?” Olek stared.

“Adaptive core. I have identified your intent as benevolent.” A holographic schematic unfurled. “This facility is a nexus. Its core stabilizes Xylos III’s seismic activity. Thorne seeks to weaponize this power.”

Tess’s old passenger felt suddenly small. The moon itself could tear. “We have to stop them,” Olek said, miner’s grit.

Chime gestured to a precarious conduit. “If the primary regulator fails, the core destabilizes. Catastrophic events will ensue.”

Drones intensified. Grish’s team pushed the outer hull. A violent tremor shook the chamber. Rocks rained. Careless work had wounded a support. The moon coughed.

“The conduit is overloading,” Chime warned, notes frantic.

Tess looked at Olek, at Chime. They believed in her. The abyss was no longer dark water. It was a job with her name on it.

“Olek, divert the inflow through the old seismic vents.” Her voice held. The knot in her stomach stayed, squeezed now by responsibility.

“I can.” He scrambled for a tunnel he knew by smell.

“Chime, guide me to the emergency seal. I need to reroute the flow. Fast.” She pushed off a crystalline pillar. Shadows no longer asked her to freeze.

She was not a soldier or a technician. She was a scavenger who knew these submerged passages like the back of her hand. She navigated the flooded corridors, the hum of the lab a beacon, Chime zipping ahead, lights flashing, a silver guardian. The pressure mounted, not just from the water, but from the knowledge that the moon’s fate rested on her shoulders. She remembered Thorne’s sneering face, the corporate ambition that threatened everything, and swam past it.

She reached a chamber pulsing with raw energy. Wires sparked. Coolant hissed. Grish and his thugs were trying to force their way in, brute strength no match for the finesse required. “Not today, Thorne,” Tess grunted, pushing past them, movements fluid, the old passenger a distant echo. She had faced her abyss, and it was the greed of men, not the depth of the ocean. With Chime’s rapid precise instructions she worked the controls, fingers flying across alien interfaces, each touch a gamble. Olek’s diversion echoed through the tunnels, a counter-rhythm to the overloading conduit, and the tremors began to subside. The conduit stabilized. Frantic overload became a steady powerful thrum.

“Seal engaged. Nexus power rerouted. Core integrity maintained,” Chime said, notes soft.

Thorne’s damaged sub retreated into murk. Grish’s team waited in a flooded antechamber, swagger replaced by complaints.

Exhausted but exhilarated, Tess floated in the now-calm water, the hum of the precursor lab a lullaby of safety. Olek surfaced beside her, grinning, his face streaked with grime but alight with triumph.

“You did it, Tess,” he said, awe in his voice. “You faced the deep and won. You saved us all.”

Tess looked back at the lab, crystalline panels glowing softly, a beacon of hope. The darkness no longer held terror, but the promise of a future protected. She had begun by fearing the void. She finished as someone who would dive it again, on purpose, a guardian of secrets on Xylos III. The moon, and Tess, were safe.
characters: Tess (scavenger diver), Olek (miner's son), Chime (pressure-suit assistant)
